pages.think: Hoje você pede um café e entende o preço.

pages.hook: In the USA, a coffee shop is a place for small, fast, friendly conversations. Learn how it really works before you step up to the counter.

facts.label: The question you always hear
facts.sub: “For here” = a mug · “To go” = a paper cup with a lid

facts.label: A normal tip
facts.sub: Usually in a tip jar or on the card screen, mostly at sit-down service

facts.label: On the cup
facts.sub: Baristas often ask for your name and write it on the cup

facts.label: Queue habits
facts.sub: People wait in line, order, step to the side and wait for their name

facts.label: Milk, size, hot or iced
facts.sub: Asking for changes is normal: “Could you make it decaf?”

pages.polite: Say **please** and **thanks**. “Can I get…?” is very common; **“I’d like…”** sounds a bit more polite.

mythfact.s: In the USA you only say “Coffee” and point.
mythfact.why: People use full requests like “Can I get a coffee, please?”

mythfact.s: Baristas often ask for your name.
mythfact.why: They write it on the cup so they can call you when it is ready.

mythfact.s: “For here” means you take the drink away.
mythfact.why: “For here” = you stay. “To go” = you leave.

mythfact.s: It is normal to ask for oat milk or decaf.
mythfact.why: Customizing a drink is part of the culture.

decode.q: How much is a medium iced latte with oat milk?
decode.why: $5 for the medium latte + $0.75 for oat milk = $5.75.

lines: Hi! I’d like to order for pickup.

decode.q: What time will the customer pick it up?

compare.br: In Brazil many people just say “Um café, por favor” and pay at the counter, often standing and chatting with the staff.
compare.us: In the USA you give a full, polite request, wait for your name to be called and often tip a little for the barista.
compare.tip: A full request is not “too much”: it is simply how people are polite in English.
compare.ask: What do you say when you order coffee where you live? Say it in English.

quiz.q: “For here or to go?” — you want to leave with your coffee. You say…
quiz.why: Answer the question directly: To go, please.

quiz.q: A natural, polite way to order is…
opts: Can I get a coffee, please?
quiz.why: Can I get… + please is natural and polite.

quiz.q: Why does the barista write your name on the cup?
opts: To call you when it is ready
quiz.why: So they can call your name when the drink is ready.

pages.title: Reading quest — My first coffee shop in New York
text: When I arrived in **New York**, I wanted a coffee. I walked into a small café near my hotel. The line was long, but it moved fast.

At the counter, the barista smiled and said, “**What can I get for you?**” I was nervous, so I said, “**Can I get** a small coffee, please?” She asked, “**For here or to go?**” I said, “**To go**, please.”
Then she asked my name. “It’s Ana,” I said. She wrote “Anna” on the cup! I laughed. When my coffee was ready, she called, “**Anna!**” and I picked it up.
I also wanted to try something new, so I asked, “**Do you have** oat milk?” “Yes, we do!” she said. It cost 75 cents extra. I paid by card and left a small tip.

Before I left, I watched the people around me. A man ordered an **iced latte** with **oat milk**; a student asked, “**Do you have** a muffin?”; and two friends said, “**That’s all**, thanks.” Everyone used short, polite sentences, and nobody seemed in a hurry.
My first coffee in New York was not perfect, but it was great. Now I know the magic words: **please**, **thanks** and **to go**.
